summary: This standards-track memo defines the IPSECKEY resource record, a DNS record type for storing public keys used by IPsec. The record can also say which gateway should be contacted when an IPsec tunnel is set up. It replaces the older approach of keeping such keys in KEY records.

plainLanguage.summary: The phone book of the Internet, DNS, can also hold a lock that others use to send you secret messages. This record stores that lock and tells people where to knock.

subtitle: A DNS record type that publishes the public key, and optionally the gateway, for setting up an IPsec tunnel.

tldr.problem: A host that wants an IPsec tunnel to a remote entity needs that entity's public key to authenticate it, and may need to know whether to contact it directly or go through a gateway.
tldr.mechanism: The IPSECKEY resource record (type 45) stores a precedence, a gateway type, an algorithm type, an optional gateway and a public key under a DNS name, often a reverse-lookup name.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the functionality of sub-type 4 of the KEY record, which RFC 3445 had obsoleted, and should be used with DNSSEC or another way to authenticate the record.

today: RFC 4025 is a Proposed Standard from 2005, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Keys Go in DNS
sections.content:
Suppose a host wants, or is required by policy, to set up an IPsec tunnel with a remote entity before normal communication begins. The host may learn the remote DNS name directly, from a PTR query on an IP address, or from the DNS part of a user@FQDN name. It then needs a public key to authenticate the remote entity, and may need guidance on whether to contact it directly or use another node as a gateway.

The IPSECKEY resource record stores that information. Its type number is 45. The key can belong to a host, a network, or an application (in the case of per-port keying). The record replaces the functionality of sub-type 4 of the KEY record, which was obsoleted by RFC 3445.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two computers can talk secretly, one needs the other's public lock. This record is a place in DNS to look the lock up.

sections.title: Looking Records Up and Using Them
sections.content:
A security gateway often has only an IP address, so the best way to find IPSECKEY records is frequently the reverse mapping trees: IN-ADDR.ARPA for IPv4 and IP6.ARPA for IPv6. The lookup works as for PTR records, with the octets (IPv4) or nibbles (IPv6) reversed. Any CNAMEs or DNAMEs found MUST be followed. Using the forward name is not precluded when it is available.

An IPSECKEY record SHOULD be used with DNSSEC unless some other means of authenticating it is available. Several records at one name are expected, because of multiple gateways and key rollover. The record is class independent.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only know a house number, you can flip it around and look it up in a special reverse section of the phone book. The key can be found there too.

sections.title: The IPSECKEY Record Format
sections.content:
The record data holds a precedence, a gateway type, an algorithm type, an optional gateway and a public key.

  • Precedence is 8 bits and works like the PREFERENCE field in RFC 1035. Gateways with lower precedence are tried first, and ties are ordered non-deterministically.
  • Gateway type: 0 no gateway, 1 a 4-byte IPv4 address, 2 a 16-byte IPv6 address, 3 a wire-encoded domain name that MUST NOT be compressed.
  • Algorithm type: 0 no key, 1 a DSA key as in RFC 2536, 2 an RSA key as in RFC 3110.
  • Gateway says where an IPsec tunnel may be created to reach the named entity.

Public keys reuse the algorithm-specific part of the KEY record data, which is everything after its first four octets. For RSA, the IPSECKEY record sets no length limit beyond the 65535 octet limit from the two-octet length encoding. That extension applies only to IPSECKEY, not to KEY records.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry is a small form: how important this entry is, what kind of address the front desk has, what kind of lock it is, and then the lock itself.

sections.title: Presentation Format and Examples
sections.content:
In a zone master file, the precedence, gateway type, algorithm and gateway fields are REQUIRED. The base64 public key is OPTIONAL; if absent, the key field is zero octets long. The algorithm is an unsigned integer with no mnemonics. If no gateway is indicated, the gateway type MUST be zero and the gateway field MUST be .. Whitespace is allowed within the base64 text.

The RFC gives examples for a node at 192.0.2.38 that accepts tunnels itself, one that only publishes its key, and ones that delegate to a gateway by IPv4 address, by domain name (mygateway.example.com) or, for an IPv6 node, by IPv6 address.
sections.plainLanguage: In the written-down version, you fill in the same form as numbers and a long jumble for the lock. A single dot means there is no front desk.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The record SHOULD reach the end client without modification. The trust channel is up to the consumer and may be end-to-end DNSSEC validation, a TSIG or SIG(0) channel, a secure local channel, or a combination. The keying material is not sensitive to passive attacks and may be freely disclosed.

An attacker who can modify DNS replies could replace the key, which leads to a denial of service unless the attacker is also a man-in-the-middle on IKE. Replacing the gateway address is easier, since the attacker need not be on the forwarding path. To defend against this, if the record's integrity is suspect, the client MUST restrict use to cases where the record owner name matches the gateway field (a null gateway counts as a match). Records obtained under unverified conditions with a non-null gateway MUST be ignored. For gateway type 3, the record MUST be ignored whenever the resulting gateway does not match the QNAME of the original query.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock is not secret, but a trickster could swap the front desk address in the phone book. Without a trustworthy phone book, only believe entries that point back to the same name.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: IANA assigns type 45 to the IPSECKEY record in the DNS resource record types registry. Two new registries are created, both specific to this record. For the algorithm type field, values 0, 1 and 2 are defined and 3 through 255 can be assigned by IETF Consensus. For the gateway type field, values 0, 1, 2 and 3 are defined and 4 through 255 can be assigned by Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: The number-keeper keeps two lists, one for lock types and one for address types, and decides who may add new entries.

items.desc: A wire-encoded domain name that must not be compressed.
